stem: An analyst can see failed logins on a domain controller, a privilege change on a file server, and a large outbound transfer on the firewall, but each is in a separate console. Which capability would BEST allow these to be seen as a single attack pattern?

options.text: A SIEM that centrally collects and correlates events across the sources
options.rationale: Cross-source correlation is exactly what a SIEM provides, turning isolated events into a detectable multi-step attack.

options.text: A longer log retention period on each individual host
options.rationale: Retention preserves data but does nothing to correlate events scattered across separate consoles.

options.text: Enabling more verbose logging on each device
options.rationale: More detail per device does not connect events across devices; without correlation the pattern remains invisible.

options.text: A faster network link between the sites
options.rationale: Bandwidth is irrelevant to correlating and analyzing security events.

stem: During an investigation, logs from three servers cannot be reliably sequenced because their timestamps disagree by minutes. To fix this going forward, what should be implemented FIRST?

options.text: Synchronize all system clocks using NTP
options.rationale: Accurate correlation depends on synchronized clocks; NTP is the foundational fix that makes timestamps comparable across systems.

options.text: Increase the log verbosity on all three servers
options.rationale: More detail does not resolve mismatched timestamps that prevent sequencing.

options.text: Store logs in a single spreadsheet
options.rationale: Aggregating into a spreadsheet does not correct inconsistent time sources and is not sound log management.

options.text: Encrypt the log files at rest
options.rationale: Encryption protects confidentiality but has no effect on timestamp accuracy or sequencing.

stem: After compromising a server, an attacker cleared its local security logs to hide their tracks. Which control would BEST prevent this from destroying the evidence next time?

options.text: Forward logs in near-real-time to a protected, centralized (write-once) log server
options.rationale: Centralized, tamper-resistant remote logging means a compromised host cannot erase the copies already sent off-box.

options.text: Store logs only on the local host but with stricter file permissions
options.rationale: An attacker with administrative control of the host can override local permissions and still clear the logs.

options.text: Reduce the amount of logging to make logs harder to find
options.rationale: Logging less weakens detection and does nothing to protect the logs from a privileged attacker.

options.text: Rotate the local logs more frequently
options.rationale: Frequent rotation on the same compromised host does not protect logs from deletion and may even purge evidence sooner.

stem: An organization wants to detect when a legitimate user's account begins behaving abnormally — accessing systems it never touches and downloading unusually large volumes. Which technology is BEST suited to this?

options.text: User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA)
options.rationale: UEBA baselines normal behavior per user/entity and flags deviations, which is ideal for detecting compromised or misused accounts.

options.text: A signature-based antivirus scanner
options.rationale: Signature AV detects known malware files, not anomalous account behavior with legitimate credentials.

options.text: A stateful packet-filtering firewall
options.rationale: A firewall enforces traffic rules but does not baseline user behavior to spot anomalies.

options.text: A vulnerability scanner
options.rationale: Vulnerability scanners find weaknesses in systems, not abnormal user activity.

stem: A security team is most concerned about sensitive data being smuggled out of the network. Which monitoring approach BEST targets this risk?

options.text: Egress monitoring combined with DLP inspection of outbound traffic
options.rationale: Egress monitoring/DLP inspects data leaving the network, directly addressing exfiltration and C2 concerns.

options.text: Reviewing inbound firewall deny logs
options.rationale: Inbound deny logs show blocked incoming traffic, not sensitive data leaving the organization.

options.text: Hardening host baselines
options.rationale: Baseline hardening reduces attack surface but does not monitor for data leaving the network.

options.text: Increasing password complexity requirements
options.rationale: Stronger passwords help authentication but do not detect outbound data exfiltration.

stem: Analysts are overwhelmed by thousands of low-value SIEM alerts per day and are beginning to ignore them, risking missed true positives. What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.text: Tune the correlation rules and set clipping levels/thresholds to suppress routine noise
options.rationale: Tuning and thresholds reduce false positives and alert fatigue so analysts can focus on meaningful alerts, the core remedy for alert overload.

options.text: Disable the SIEM until analysts have more time
options.rationale: Disabling detection eliminates visibility entirely and is far worse than tuning the noise.

options.text: Hire enough analysts to read every single alert
options.rationale: Staffing to read unfiltered noise is inefficient and unsustainable; the root problem is untuned rules, not headcount.

options.text: Route all alerts straight to executive email
options.rationale: Forwarding unfiltered noise elsewhere spreads alert fatigue rather than solving it.

stem: Which statement BEST describes continuous monitoring?

options.text: Ongoing, largely automated assessment of security controls and configurations against a defined baseline
options.rationale: Continuous monitoring provides near-real-time posture assessment rather than relying on periodic, point-in-time audits.

options.text: An annual manual audit performed by external assessors
options.rationale: An annual point-in-time audit is the opposite of the ongoing, automated nature of continuous monitoring.

options.text: Encrypting all data in transit and at rest
options.rationale: Encryption is a protective control, not a monitoring activity that assesses control state over time.

options.text: Blocking all outbound traffic by default
options.rationale: Default-deny egress is a network control, not the practice of continuously assessing posture.

stem: An auditor finds a company generates comprehensive logs but has no process to review them. From a detection standpoint, what is the MOST significant weakness?

options.text: The logs provide little detection value because no monitoring/review occurs
options.rationale: Logging realizes security value only through active review or correlation; unread logs rarely lead to timely detection.

options.text: The logs are too detailed and should be reduced
options.rationale: Detail is not the core issue; the absence of any review is, and reducing detail would not add detection.

options.text: The logs consume too much storage
options.rationale: Storage cost is a secondary concern next to the fact that no one is monitoring the logs at all.

options.text: The logs should be printed to paper for safekeeping
options.rationale: Printing is impractical and still would not create a review/monitoring process.

stem: What does a SIEM do when it normalizes log data?

options.text: Converts logs from many formats into a consistent structure so they can be compared and correlated
options.rationale: Normalization standardizes disparate log formats into a common schema, enabling correlation across sources.

options.text: Deletes duplicate logs to save storage space
options.rationale: Deduplication is a separate function; normalization is about standardizing format, not removing duplicates.

options.text: Encrypts logs before they are stored
options.rationale: Encryption is a protection step, not what normalization means.

options.text: Compresses logs to reduce bandwidth
options.rationale: Compression reduces size but is not the definition of normalization.

stem: A database administrator with legitimate access begins querying customer records at 3 a.m. and exporting far more than usual over several nights. Which monitoring capability would BEST have flagged this insider activity?

options.text: UEBA detecting deviation from the DBA's established behavioral baseline
options.rationale: Because the access is authorized, only behavior-based analytics that baseline normal activity would flag the off-hours, high-volume anomaly.

options.text: An access control list denying the DBA access
options.rationale: The DBA has legitimate access needed for the job; denying it would break operations and is not a monitoring capability.

options.text: A signature-based IDS matching known exploit patterns
options.rationale: No exploit signature is triggered; the activity uses valid credentials and normal queries, defeating signature matching.

options.text: A spam filter on the email gateway
options.rationale: Email filtering is unrelated to detecting anomalous database access by an insider.

stem: A CISO wants assurance that logs remain trustworthy even if an endpoint is fully compromised. Which design BEST achieves this?

options.text: Stream logs off the host immediately to a central, append-only log repository
options.rationale: Getting logs off the endpoint to append-only central storage protects them from deletion by an attacker who owns the host.

options.text: Rely on local log files with audit-only file permissions
options.rationale: A privileged attacker on the host can bypass local permissions and delete or alter the logs.

options.text: Keep logs only in volatile memory for speed
options.rationale: Memory-only logs are lost on reboot or compromise and provide no durable, tamper-resistant record.

options.text: Disable logging during incidents to avoid tampering
options.rationale: Disabling logging during an incident removes exactly the evidence needed to investigate it.

stem: Malware on an internal host is beaconing to an external command-and-control server and slowly uploading stolen files. Which monitoring focus is MOST likely to catch this?

options.text: Egress (outbound) traffic monitoring
options.rationale: C2 beaconing and data uploads are outbound behaviors, so inspecting egress traffic is the most direct way to detect them.

options.text: Inbound intrusion prevention on the perimeter
options.rationale: Inbound IPS focuses on incoming attacks and is less effective at spotting established outbound C2 and exfiltration.

options.text: Physical access logs at the data center
options.rationale: Physical access records are unrelated to detecting network-based C2 and exfiltration.

options.text: Password vault access reports
options.rationale: Vault access reports track credential retrieval, not outbound malicious traffic.

stem: A user's credentials are used to log in from two countries within ten minutes ('impossible travel'). Which tool is BEST positioned to raise this as an anomaly automatically?

options.text: UEBA analyzing login patterns against the user's behavioral baseline
options.rationale: Impossible-travel detection is a classic UEBA anomaly derived from baselining a user's normal login geography and timing.

options.text: A host-based antivirus agent
options.rationale: AV scans for malware on the endpoint and does not analyze cross-location login patterns.

options.text: A network switch's port security
options.rationale: Port security binds MAC addresses to ports locally and cannot reason about geographic login anomalies.

options.text: A patch management dashboard
options.rationale: Patch dashboards track update status, not anomalous authentication behavior.

stem: Why is NTP synchronization considered a PRIMARY prerequisite for effective log correlation across an enterprise?

options.text: Because correlating events across systems requires timestamps that are consistent and comparable
options.rationale: If clocks disagree, events cannot be reliably ordered or matched, breaking cross-system correlation and investigations.

options.text: Because NTP encrypts the log data in transit
options.rationale: NTP synchronizes time; it does not encrypt logs, so this is not why it matters for correlation.

options.text: Because NTP compresses logs to save space
options.rationale: NTP has nothing to do with compression or storage efficiency.

options.text: Because NTP authenticates users to the SIEM
options.rationale: NTP does not perform user authentication; that is unrelated to its timekeeping role.

stem: A newly deployed SIEM rule fires hundreds of times a day, almost all for benign administrator activity. What is the MOST appropriate action?

options.text: Refine the rule with thresholds/exclusions so it alerts only on genuinely suspicious activity
options.rationale: Tuning the rule to exclude known-benign behavior reduces false positives while preserving detection of true anomalies.

options.text: Delete the rule entirely
options.rationale: Deleting the rule removes the detection capability instead of improving its precision.

options.text: Ignore the alerts since most are benign
options.rationale: Blanket ignoring trains analysts to overlook the rule and risks missing the rare true positive.

options.text: Lower the SIEM's log ingestion so fewer events arrive
options.rationale: Reducing ingestion blinds the SIEM broadly rather than precisely fixing one noisy rule.

stem: An organization must decide how long to keep its security logs. Which factor BEST determines the required retention period?

options.text: Legal, regulatory, and organizational policy requirements
options.rationale: Retention periods are driven by applicable laws, regulations, and internal policy, which set minimum and sometimes maximum durations.

options.text: The amount of free disk space currently available
options.rationale: Available storage is an implementation constraint, not the authority that determines required retention.

options.text: The preference of the newest analyst on the team
options.rationale: Individual preference is not a legitimate basis for a compliance-driven retention decision.

options.text: The color scheme of the SIEM dashboard
options.rationale: This is irrelevant to retention requirements and is a distractor.

stem: Leadership wants to know, at any given moment, whether critical systems still meet their secure configuration baseline rather than waiting for the annual audit. Which practice BEST meets this need?

options.text: Continuous monitoring of configurations against the baseline
options.rationale: Continuous monitoring provides near-real-time visibility into configuration drift and control state, exactly what is requested.

options.text: A one-time penetration test
options.rationale: A point-in-time pen test does not provide ongoing, moment-to-moment posture visibility.

options.text: Quarterly awareness training
options.rationale: Training addresses human behavior, not real-time configuration compliance.

options.text: An annual policy review
options.rationale: An annual review is periodic, the opposite of continuous, and cannot show current state at any moment.

stem: In monitoring, what is a 'clipping level'?

options.text: A threshold below which routine events are treated as noise and not alerted
options.rationale: A clipping level suppresses alerts until activity exceeds a baseline count, reducing false positives from normal behavior.

options.text: The maximum size a log file may reach before rotation
options.rationale: That describes a log rotation size limit, not a clipping level for alerting.

options.text: The encryption strength applied to stored logs
options.rationale: Encryption strength is unrelated to the alerting threshold concept of a clipping level.

options.text: The number of days logs are retained
options.rationale: That is a retention period, not a clipping level.

stem: A team wants to detect an attack that unfolds as several small, individually unremarkable steps across different systems. Which approach is LEAST likely to detect it?

options.text: Reviewing each system's logs independently in isolation
options.rationale: Individually unremarkable events only reveal the attack when correlated; reviewing systems in isolation is precisely what misses the pattern.

options.text: Correlating events across systems in a SIEM
options.rationale: Cross-system correlation is well suited to surface multi-step attacks, so it is likely to detect, not miss, the pattern.

options.text: Applying UEBA to spot behavioral anomalies
options.rationale: Behavioral analytics can flag anomalous steps even when each looks benign in isolation, aiding detection.

options.text: Using a SIEM rule that links failed logins to later privilege changes
options.rationale: A correlation rule chaining related steps is designed to catch exactly this kind of multi-step activity.

stem: A company invests heavily in log collection infrastructure but assigns no one to analyze the data. What is the PRIMARY reason this investment yields little security benefit?

options.text: Detection requires active monitoring and analysis, which is absent here
options.rationale: Logs are only an enabler; without analysis or correlation they do not translate into detection or response.

options.text: The logs are being collected too quickly
options.rationale: Collection speed is not the problem; the absence of any analysis is.

options.text: Log collection inherently degrades system performance to uselessness
options.rationale: Well-designed logging has manageable overhead; performance is not why the benefit is lost.

options.text: Collecting logs automatically prevents all attacks
options.rationale: This is false; collection alone prevents nothing, which is precisely the point of the scenario.
